title: Arjuna's Divine Eye
word: each as a lens for a week
hookLine: Arjuna asks to see Krishna as he really is, and Krishna says: not with those eyes. why Hindus go to the temple to see
carry: darshana: to see and be seen; six ways of seeing
tomorrow: a rumor at the bus stop: how would Nyaya check it?

cards: On the battlefield in the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna has been listening to his friend and charioteer, Krishna, for chapters. And then he asks for something bold.
If you think I can bear it, show me your real form, your whole self. Krishna agrees, with one catch. You can't see me with these eyes of yours.
I'll give you a divine eye. And Arjuna sees: the whole universe in one body, without beginning, middle or end, brighter than a thousand suns. He's shaking.
Afterward, he begs Krishna to take his gentle, familiar form again.

teach.h: DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.
teach.b: Here's the teaching inside that story: in Hinduism, seeing is itself a sacred act. Hindus don't usually say they go to the temple just to pray. They say they go for darshan, to see the deity, and to be seen by the deity.
Standing before the image, eyes open, receiving a glance back: that is worship. Arjuna's story says something more.

teach.h: WHAT YOU SEE DEPENDS ON YOUR EYES.
teach.b: What you see depends on the eyes you bring.
The same word, darshana, names the six classical schools of Hindu thought. Each is a way of seeing. We've walked through all six, and one way to hold them is by the question each keeps asking.
Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching?
Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on?
Those are our short versions, not their own words.
Think of the eye doctor clicking lenses in: better like this, or like this? The letters don't change. What comes into focus does.

Over the next days we'll try the lenses two at a time on ordinary moments: a rumor, a flash of anger, a sink full of dishes. Not to pick a winner. This part of the path is called schools of thought, never ranked.
Like Arjuna, you're just asking for eyes that can see more.

how: Hindus go to the temple for darshan, standing before the deity to see and be seen, often timed to when the shrine's curtain opens; the six darshanas are traditionally grouped in pairs, Nyaya with Vaisheshika, Samkhya with Yoga, and Mimamsa with Vedanta.

games.q: what does “each as a lens for a week” mean?
o: trying each school's question as a way of seeing
a week of fasting to sharpen the inner eye
picking the one school that sees most clearly

games.q: ways of seeing — tap the pairs.
p: seeing the deity and being seen
what does all of it rest on?

s: for Hindus, darshan at the temple goes both ways: you see, and you're seen
standing before the deity with open eyes is itself worship.
Arjuna sees Krishna's universal form with his ordinary eyes
Krishna says he can't, and gives him a divine eye.
the six darshanas are meant to be ranked from best to worst
this part of the path holds them as lenses, never ranked.

games.q: a friend at the temple asks why everyone crowds forward when the curtain opens, instead of praying from the back. what's the answer?
o: it's just a line; there's nothing special about seeing
they've come for darshan: to see the deity and be seen
the prayers only count from the front row
games.why: darshan is the heart of temple visits: seeing is worship. the six schools take the same name: ways of seeing.

practice: If you have a deity's picture or an image at home, sit before it with your eyes open, and simply look, and let yourself be looked at. If not, look at something living, a plant, a face in a photo, the sky.
Then ask one of the six questions, softly: what does this rest on? Let it go, and keep looking. If you pray, you can let this looking be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, ways of seeing, held not as rivals but as lenses you can try one at a time. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: seeing, a view; the word for seeing the deity and for a school of thought.

carryVoice: Your line: darshana, to see and be seen; six ways of seeing. Like Arjuna, ask for new eyes. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 11.3-11.8, 11.13 and 11.16 (Arjuna asks to see Krishna's form; 'you cannot see me with these eyes; I give you a divine eye'; the whole universe in one body; no beginning, middle or end)
Bhagavad Gita 11.12 and 11.45-11.51 (brighter than a thousand suns; Arjuna, shaken, asks for the gentler form, and Krishna shows his human form again)
the six darshanas (Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta) as treated earlier in this part of the path
